1.5.2.3   Karst Areas

EGTS does not anticipate that karst features will underlie the proposed facilities. Proposed
excavations or foundation work will primarily occur in areas that have previously undergone
similar excavations and earthwork and karst features were not encountered. During construction
of the proposed TL-669 and TL-668 pipelines, EGTS will monitor clearing, grading, and trenching
activities to identify potential karst features that may have been unidentifiable on the surface
during the preconstruction survey. If features are uncovered, they will be evaluated by a
geotechnical contractor to determine the need for mitigation measures, such as stabilization.

1.5.2.4   Cultivated Areas

In actively cultivated and rotated croplands, pastures, orchards, nurseries, and residential areas,
topsoil will be removed and segregated in accordance with the FERC Plan. Typically, topsoil will
be removed over the entire width of the construction ROW. Following pipeline installation, the
subsoil will be returned to the ditch and the topsoil replaced in the area from which it was removed.
Excess rock will be removed from at least the top 12 inches of soil to the extent practical. The
size, density and distribution of rock left in construction work areas should be similar to adjacent
areas not affected by construction, unless otherwise approved in writing by the landowner. As
necessary, the working side of the ROW will be de-compacted prior to final grading and
restoration.

Where livestock fences (including electric fences) need to be cut to access the construction ROW,
EGTS will brace and secure the fencing prior to construction and repair the fences to
preconstruction condition or better during the restoration phase of the Project. Further, EGTS will
work with landowners to remove livestock to alternate fields during construction or maintain
adequate temporary fencing in grazing areas. If cattle or other livestock are present during




                                                  -22-                                Project Stratum
                                                                                      November 2026
 construction, EGTS will install temporary fencing around the ROW in areas where the pipe trench
is left open overnight.

EGTS will work with landowners to identify drain tile systems in advance of construction. Any
drain tiles will be located, monitored for damage and repaired, as needed. Following completion
of construction and restoration, EGTS will work with landowners to repair or correct tile drainage
problems due to construction of the Project.

In agricultural lands, the pipeline will be buried at depths sufficient to provide a minimum of 4 feet
of cover to avoid potential impacts associated with typical agricultural activities, such as plowing.
In consultation with landowners, the pipeline may be buried deeper in certain locations to facilitate
the passage of heavy equipment.

1.5.2.5    Residential Areas

In residential areas, construction activities will be completed as expeditiously as practicable to
minimize disturbance to residents. While constructing in these areas, EGTS will maintain access
to the residences for the duration of construction activities. Where the pipeline ROW will cross
roads necessary for access to residential properties and no alternative entrances exist, EGTS will
implement measures, such as plating over the open portion of the trench, to maintain passage for
landowners and emergency vehicles.

In general, EGTS will reduce the width of the construction ROW or adjust the pipeline centerline
to avoid occupied structures. For residences within 50 feet of a construction work area, EGTS will
implement the following mitigation measures during construction:

   •      Install construction fencing at the edge of the construction work area for a distance of
          100 feet on either side of the residence, and maintaining the fencing throughout the open
          trench phases of construction; and
   •      Complete final cleanup near the area as quickly as possible to minimize landowner affect
          to the greatest extent practical.

EGTS will prepare site-specific construction plans for residences located within 50 feet of the
construction work areas for the Project (see Resource Report 8). The plans will identify the
mitigation measures EGTS will implement at each residence to promote safe and efficient pipeline
installation with minimal impact on residents.

Prior to construction, EGTS will take pictures or shoot video of residential properties to assist in
post-construction restoration. Following construction, debris will be removed and residential
properties will be restored as practicable to preconstruction condition or as negotiated with the
landowner. EGTS will coordinate with residential landowners to attempt to meet special requests
regarding restoration.

1.5.2.6    Rock Removal

Although shallow bedrock may be encountered in certain areas during installation of the TL-669
and TL-668 pipelines or New Terrain M&R Facility and Pipeline Tap, EGTS has indicated that
blasting should not be required for the Project. Due to the presence of existing buried pipelines
and aboveground facilities, if rock or rocky formations are encountered, EGTS will use hydraulic
hammers, tractor-mounted mechanical rippers, and/or rock trenchers for breaking up the rock

 prior to excavation. The technique selected will depend on rock properties such as relative
hardness, fracture susceptibility, expected volume, and location.

1.5.2.7    Concrete Coating

Concrete coating or bag weights may be used to provide negative buoyancy for the TL-669 and
TL-668 pipelines where installed across wetlands and waterbodies. Concrete coating, where
required, will be applied to pipe joints at the coating mill, the CYs, or on the construction ROW.
All applications of concrete coating on the construction ROW will be conducted in accordance
with a Preparedness, Prevention, and Contingency Plan (PPC Plan) to be provided by EGTS and
on-site during construction. Concrete coating activities will not be conducted within 100 feet of
wetlands, waterbodies, or springs.

1.5.3     Aboveground Facility Construction Procedures

1.5.3.1    Existing Aboveground Facility and Koppel Junction Modifications

Modifications to or associated with the existing Greenlick and Leidy Tie-Ins, Sabinsville Station,
and Koppel Junction will occur concurrently with construction of the TL-669 and TL-668 pipelines.
The construction methods for these facilities will be similar and include a standard sequence of
events. Construction will begin with the clearing and grading of the sites to establish level grades
for the facilities, if necessary. Subsequent construction activities may include:

   •      Preparing foundations;
   •      Installing underground piping;
   •      Erecting and installing buildings and auxiliary equipment;
   •      Installing and testing aboveground piping, electrical and control equipment;
   •      Cleaning up the work area;
   •      Paving or graveling permanent access roads, operational footprints, and parking areas;
          and
   •      Installing security fence, if not already in a fenced area.

Once construction is complete, disturbed areas that are not covered with foundations, paving, or
gravel will be finish-graded and seeded. Any new equipment or buildings will be fenced for security
(if not already in a fenced area), and safety and control devices will be installed and tested.

1.5.3.2    New Terrain M&R Facility and Pipeline Tap and New Gate Facilities

Construction of the New Terrain M&R Facility and Pipeline Tap and new gate facilities (Pine
Mountain Gate Facility and Eaglerock Gate Facility) will occur at the same time as construction
of the TL-669 and TL-668 pipelines. Construction activities will include clearing and grading,
installation and testing of piping and equipment, cleaning up the work area, graveling the site, and
fencing the facilities.

1.7    CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATIONS WORKFORCE

EGTS estimates that approximately 360 construction workers will be required for the Project
between Q1 2028 and Q4 2028. This includes approximately 250 workers for construction of the
TL-668 pipeline (including tie-in facilities at Leidy and Greenlick Stations and the proposed new
Pine Mountain Gate Facility) and approximately 70 workers for construction of the TL-669 pipeline
(including facilities at Koppel Junction and the proposed new Eaglerock Gate Facility). The
remaining workforce will support construction of the new M&R Facility and Pipeline Tap
(approximately 20 workers) and the proposed improvements at Sabinsville Station (approximately
20 workers).

The workforce for the Project will include superintendents, foremen, equipment operators,
laborers, construction craft inspectors, and Environmental Inspectors (EIs). Additional
construction personnel associated with survey, testing, and specialized construction methods
may also be assigned to assist with construction of the proposed Project. The composition of the
workforce will depend primarily on the contractor selected to perform the work, and EGTS will
likely bid the work to both local and non-local contractors. Any contractor would be encouraged
to hire local workers to support their workforce. EGTS anticipates that workers will utilize existing
temporary housing, such as houses, hotels, motels, campgrounds, and recreational vehicle parks.
No temporary work camps are anticipated for the Project. EGTS estimates that approximately 2
percent of the workers or inspectors required for construction of the Project will be workers who
reside within commuting distances of the Project or are members of a local union hall. The
remaining 75 percent are expected to be non-local workers who temporarily relocate to the Project
area for the period of construction.

The Project is not expected to create new permanent jobs to support the operation and
maintenance of the Project facilities. Additional information on the Project workforce is included
in Resource Report 5.

 1.8.1   Environmental Compliance

EGTS will incorporate relevant environmental requirements, and environmental mitigation plans
into the construction bid documents for the Project. Additionally, EGTS will review these materials
with prospective contractors in a pre-bid meeting. These steps, notwithstanding the contractor(s)

1.8.3   Environmental Inspection

EGTS will assign an appropriate number of EIs to monitor environmental compliance during
construction. The EIs will have peer status with other inspectors and will report directly to the

monitoring compliance with all environmental requirements of the Certificates as well as federal
and state permits, clearances, and other approvals; evaluating the construction contractor's
implementation of environmental mitigation measures; issuing corrective action and stop-activity
orders to maintain environmental compliance; documenting compliance with the environmental

environmental staff. The EIs will also act as liaisons between EGTS and field representatives of
environmental regulatory agencies that visit the Project area during construction. The EIs will
have the authority to stop construction, if necessary, to maintain environmental compliance.

1.9     OPERATIONS AND MAINTENANCE

EGTS will operate and maintain the new TL-669 and TL-668 pipelines and aboveground facilities
in accordance with all applicable federal and state requirements, including the minimum federal
safety standards identified in the Transportation of Natural and Other Gas by Pipeline, 49 CFR
192. Operation and maintenance of the Project facilities will be performed by or at the direction of
EGTS.

The USDOT’s Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulates the operation
and maintenance of natural gas pipeline facilities. The regulations found at 49 CFR 192.613,
192.703, 192.705, and 192.709 address aerial and ground patrols of pipeline facilities. EGTS will
conduct regular aerial and ground patrols of the proposed TL-669 and TL-668 pipelines in
accordance with these regulations. The frequency of patrols is determined by class location unit
(i.e., population density) and the location of the pipeline. EGTS has Standard Operating
Procedures for its facilities that define patrol frequency and methods and identify reporting


                                                 -27-                               Project Stratum
                                                                                    November 2026
 requirements for abnormal or unusual conditions. All patrols are documented in an Inspection
Monitoring System Compliance Database.

The proposed TL-669 and TL-668 pipelines, in addition to the associated tie-in and gate facilities,
will be inspected by qualified personnel from the air (quarterly) and on foot (yearly) by following
the applicable regulations. Aerial patrols will be completed by aircraft at a typical altitude ranging
between 200 and 500 feet above the ground surface. This will allow for adequate viewing of the
ROW and use of forward-looking infrared technology for leak detection. Foot patrols are
conducted by staff trained to identify potential issues such as erosion, slips, and leaks. These
surveillance activities will provide information on possible encroachments and nearby
construction activities, exposed pipe, and other potential concerns that may affect the safety and
operation of the pipelines. Field personnel will advise the appropriate operations personnel of new
construction along or near the pipeline system. Line patrol of highway and railroad crossings will
be completed as required by the USDOT. Valves will be inspected annually and the results
documented.

Pipeline markers and signs will be inspected to ensure that pipeline locations are clearly identified.
The condition of pipeline markers will be noted during line patrols, as well as during road crossing,
One-Call, and other inspections. Damaged or missing line markers will be noted and repaired or
replaced as necessary.

In order to maintain accessibility of the ROW and accommodate pipeline integrity surveys,
vegetation along the ROW will be cleared periodically, and as necessary, in accordance with the
FERC Plan and Procedures. Active cropland will be allowed to revert to preconstruction use for
the full width of the ROW. In non-cultivated uplands, the permanent easement for each pipeline
will be maintained in an herbaceous state. In wetlands, the FERC Procedures allow for a
10-foot-wide corridor centered over the pipeline to be permanently maintained in an herbaceous
state. Additionally, the FERC Procedures allow trees greater than 15 feet in height within 15 feet
of the pipeline to be cut and removed from wetlands along the ROW. Where necessary and when
required, EGTS will use mechanical mowing or cutting along the ROW for normal vegetation
maintenance.

EGTS will adhere to the operations and maintenance procedures described in the FERC Plan
and Procedures, subject to modifications approved by the FERC, in the vicinity of wetlands,
waterbodies, and upland areas. Additionally, operations and maintenance procedures, including
record keeping, will be performed in accordance with USDOT requirements. Operation and
maintenance of valves and equipment will be performed in accordance with information provided
by the manufacturers.

Pipeline integrity surveys and vegetation maintenance may identify areas along the ROW where
permanent erosion control devices need to be repaired or additional erosion control devices may
be needed. If problem areas are evident, erosion control devices will be repaired or installed, as
necessary, and the ROW will be stabilized to prevent future degradation.

EGTS’s aboveground non-pipeline facilities will be constructed, operated, and maintained in
accordance with USDOT regulations in 49 CFR 192, the Commission’s guidance in 18 CFR
380.15, and EGTS’s construction and restoration procedures outlined in this application. EGTS
personnel will perform regular operation and maintenance activities on equipment at the Project
Stratum aboveground facilities. These activities will include calibration, inspection, and scheduled
and routine maintenance. Operational testing will be performed on safety equipment to confirm
proper functioning and, as needed, corrective action.

1.10    NON-JURISDICTIONAL FACILITIES

on the public convenience and necessity of a proposed action as part of its decision to authorize
interstate natural gas facilities. Occasionally, projects reviewed by the Commission have
associated facilities that do not fall under the jurisdiction of the Commission. These “non-
jurisdictional” facilities may be integral to the need for a project (e.g., a power plant to be built at
the end of a FERC-jurisdictional pipeline); or they may be associated as minor components that
would be built as a result of the jurisdictional facilities (e.g., an electric distribution line providing
service to a natural gas compressor station).

There is one non-jurisdictional facility associated with the Project: the utility power connection for
the proposed New Terrain M&R Facility and Pipeline Tap, as described below.

1.15   ENVIRONMENTAL TRENDS AND PLANNED ACTIVITIES

This section characterizes the existing environment in the Project area, describes how the
environment has changed over time, and identifies other reasonably foreseeable projects in the
vicinity of the proposed Project.

1.15.1 Environmental Trends

The Project area is located within portions of Beaver, Lawrence, Clinton, Tioga, and Potter
Counties in PA. The counties have a humid continental climate characterized by cold winters,
warm to hot summers, and year-round precipitation. Conditions are mildest in Beaver and
Lawrence Counties to the west and become cooler and snowier toward Clinton, Potter, and Tioga
Counties, which lie on the higher plateau to the north and east (Smith 1982; Steputis et al. 1966;
Goodman et al. 1958).

All five counties are located within the Appalachian Plateaus physiographic province, which is
characterized by sedimentary bedrock, dissected uplands, narrow stream valleys, and locally
steep relief (Sevon 2000). Beaver and Lawrence Counties lie within the Pittsburgh Low Plateau
Section, characterized by a smooth to irregular, undulating surface with narrow, relatively shallow
valleys and elevations ranging from 660 to 2,340 feet above mean sea level (AMSL). The
underlying bedrock consists of cyclic sequences of sandstone, shale, limestone, clay, and coal
(USGS 2026). Both counties are within the Ohio River basin.

Clinton and Potter Counties lie within the Deep Valleys Section, characterized by very deep,
angular valleys and broad to narrow uplands, with elevations ranging from 560 to 2,560 feet
AMSL. The underlying bedrock consists of sandstone, siltstone, and shale (USGS 2026). Both
counties are within the Susquehanna River basin.

Tioga County lies within the Glaciated High Plateau Section, characterized by broad to narrow,
rounded to flat uplands and shallow valleys shaped by fluvial and glacial erosion and glacial

 deposition. Elevations range from approximately 620 to 2,560 feet AMSL, and the underlying
bedrock consists of sandstone, siltstone, shale, and some coal and conglomerate (USGS 2026).
The county is within the Susquehanna River Basin.

These geologic and landform conditions historically influenced settlement, transportation,
agriculture, and resource extraction throughout the Project area. Beaver County, formed in 1800,
developed around the confluence of the Beaver and Ohio Rivers, which supported transportation,
agriculture, and water-powered mills and factories. The county’s natural resources included oil,
limestone, sandstone, and coal (Smith 1982). Lawrence County, formed in 1849, developed
around New Castle at the junction of the Shenango River and Neshannock Creek, where canal
transportation and tin plate mills supported manufacturing and population growth (Smith 1982).
In Clinton County, settlement concentrated on fertile land along the West Branch Susquehanna
River and canal, while subsequent railroad development supported the lumber industry (Maynard
1985). Potter and Tioga Counties, both formed in 1804, experienced substantial resource-driven
growth. Potter County’s forests supported an extensive lumber industry during the nineteenth
century, accompanied by sawmills, tanneries, and railroads, until much of the timber had been
harvested by approximately 1912. Tioga County was a leading producer of bituminous coal from
the 1840s through the 1880s, with mining towns and railroads supporting coal extraction; its
forests also supported a substantial lumber industry (Elmira 2026).

Today, land cover in the Project counties is predominantly forested in Clinton, Potter, and Tioga
Counties, whereas Beaver and Lawrence Counties contain more agricultural and developed land
(USGS 2024). Development is concentrated in and around communities along major
transportation corridors and waterways, including the Ohio and Beaver Rivers in Beaver County;
New Castle and Ellwood City in Lawrence County; Wellsboro and Mansfield along the U.S. Route
6 corridor in Tioga County; and Coudersport in Potter County. Outside these developed areas,
pasture, hayfields, and cropland remain important rural land uses.

Population in the Project counties has declined in recent years. Between 2010 and 2022, Beaver
County decreased from 170,539 to 167,629 residents (1.7 percent); Clinton County from 39,238
to 37,860 (3.5 percent); Tioga County from 41,981 to 41,186 (1.9 percent); Lawrence County from
91,108 to 85,907 (5.7 percent); and Potter County from 17,457 to 16,390 (6.1 percent). Population
density ranges from approximately 15 persons per square mile in rural Potter County to 387
persons per square mile in Beaver County (U.S. Census Bureau 2011, 2020).

Both the Ohio and Susquehanna River basins are affected by agriculture, abandoned mine
drainage, and urban stormwater runoff (PADEP 2026). Air quality in the Project counties is
generally good; however, some areas are designated nonattainment or maintenance areas for
certain National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). Beaver County is designated
nonattainment for the 2008 8-hour ozone standard and is a maintenance area for the 2006 fine
particulate matter (PM₂.₅) standard. Portions of the county are also designated nonattainment for
the 2008 lead standard and the 2010 sulfur dioxide standard; however, the Project is not located
within these designated areas. A portion of Lawrence County is a maintenance area for the 2006
PM₂.₅ standard, but the Project is not located within that area. Clinton, Potter, and Tioga Counties
are in attainment or are unclassifiable for all active NAAQS, while Beaver and Lawrence Counties
are in attainment or are unclassifiable for all other active standards (EPA 2026).

 1.15.2 Planned Activities

In a recent FERC order pursuant to Docket No. CP25-528-000, the Commission noted in
paragraph 25 of that order, that the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”) contains no
reference to cumulative effects and that in the Commission’s view, identifying a distinct and
separate category of cumulative effects has proved to ultimately disserve NEPA’s goal of
supporting environmentally informed decision making without imposing undue procedural
burdens. Rather, the Commission identified that NEPA requires an analysis of the reasonably
foreseeable effects of “the project at hand,” not effects of separate projects. More specifically, “the
effects of a project occur against an environmental backdrop that may itself be shaped by other
activities; for that reason, information on other activities in the vicinity of a proposed project can
help the Commission contextualize and understand how that project will affect the environment.”
Consequently, EGTS is providing information on other activities in the vicinity of the proposed
Project, reflecting the “cumulative effects resulting from existing or reasonably foreseeable
projects.” 18 CFR § 380.12(b)(3).

The assessment area for other activities within the vicinity of the proposed Project includes the
area directly affected by construction of the Project facilities in addition to the anticipated area of
effect the Project may have on each resource. This assessment area varies for each resource,
based on the potential for effects to extend beyond the area of direct effect. For example, effects
on air quality have the potential to extend beyond the Project boundaries, but effects on geologic
and soil resources would likely not extend beyond the construction boundaries. Table 1.15.1-1
identifies resource-specific geographic and temporal extents used to assess potential cumulative
impacts for the proposed Project.

 As shown in Table 1.15.1-2, several planned and ongoing projects are located within the
resource-specific geographic scopes of the proposed Project and are anticipated to occur
between 2026 and the scheduled in-service date of the EGTS facilities in Q2 2028. Of these
projects, the Switch Data Center Campus is adjacent to and north of the proposed TL-669
pipeline; the SR 18 (Big Beaver Boulevard) project is located approximately 0.19 mile north of the
proposed TL-669 pipeline; and the Capital Area Project and Project Oak Leaf are located adjacent
to the existing Leidy Station. Other planned projects in the area include the Aligned Data Centers
campus, Shell Chemical Appalachia plant upgrades, and the Shippingport Lateral Project in
Beaver County; the Winner Solar Project in Clinton County; the Tioga Pathway Project in Potter
and Tioga Counties; municipal sewer and storm sewer improvements in Lawrence County; and
numerous PennDOT bridge replacement and roadway projects throughout the five counties. Most
of these projects are located more than 9 miles from the proposed Project facilities.

Construction of projects within the resource-specific geographic scopes could contribute to
temporary, localized impacts on soils, vegetation, surface water, wetlands, and other resources
evaluated for the proposed Project. The potential for overlapping impacts would be greatest where
projects are immediately adjacent to proposed Project facilities and construction schedules
overlap. Potential overlapping impacts could include temporary increases in soil disturbance,
vegetation clearing, stormwater runoff, construction traffic, noise, and air emissions.

The potential for overlapping impacts would be limited by the localized nature and temporary
duration of construction activities, the distance between most identified projects and the proposed
Project facilities, and the implementation of applicable environmental protection, permitting, and
mitigation measures. Based on these considerations, the combined impacts of the identified
projects and Project Stratum are not anticipated to result in measurable adverse impacts on the
resources evaluated.

 2.0       RESOURCE REPORT 2 – WATER USE AND QUALITY

 Eastern Gas Transmission and Storage, Inc. (EGTS) is seeking a Certificate of Public
 Convenience and Necessity from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) under
 Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act, as amended, for the proposed Project Stratum (Project). The
 Project is designed to provide 250,000 dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of incremental, year-round
 firm natural gas transportation capacity to meet growing energy needs in Pennsylvania (PA) and
 enhance the flexibility and reliability of the EGTS system. To provide the incremental capacity,
 EGTS will leverage existing infrastructure, including receipt point Metering and Regulation (M&R)
 facilities and compressor stations, in addition to installing new pipeline, completing upgrades at
 existing stations, and constructing new supporting facilities. The incremental capacity would
 support deliveries to Lawrence and Clinton Counties, PA.

 The proposed Project facilities include the following:

 Pipeline Facilities:
    • TL-669 Natural Gas Transmission Line: install approximately 1.8 miles of new 24-inch
        outside diameter steel natural gas pipeline originating from the existing Koppel Junction
        and extending northwest to the proposed Eaglerock Gate Facility in Beaver County, PA.
        The pipeline will be co-located with the existing EGTS LN-25 and LN-35 natural gas
        pipelines.
      •   TL-668 Natural Gas Transmission Line: install approximately 13.8 miles of new 24-inch
          outside diameter steel natural gas pipeline originating from a tie-in at the existing Leidy
          Station in Clinton County, PA to a tie-in at the proposed Pine Mountain Gate Facility in
          Potter County, PA. The pipeline will be co-located with several other EGTS pipelines and
          will replace the existing LN-280/LN-340 pipelines along the proposed TL-668 alignment.

 Existing Aboveground Facilities:
    • Sabinsville Station Improvements: complete various modifications and improvements at
        the existing Sabinsville Station to support the Project which may involve replacements,
        upgrades, or rearrangements of station piping, pressure control systems, miscellaneous
        pipeline components and valves, and supporting infrastructure. The proposed
        improvements will occur within the existing facility footprint or within existing permanent
        pipeline ROW in Tioga County, PA.
      •   Leidy Station Tie-In: install a new tie-in facility that will connect the TL-668 to the existing
          TL-454 and LN-50 pipelines and include launcher/receivers and associated
          appurtenances. The proposed improvements will occur within the existing Leidy Station
          facility footprint in Clinton County, PA.
      •   Greenlick Station Tie-In: install new zone measurement equipment, a mainline valve
          assembly, and tie-ins to existing Greenlick Station piping. The proposed modifications will
          be installed within the existing pipeline ROW adjacent to the Greenlick Station in Potter
          County, PA.
      •   Koppel Junction Improvements: install a new launcher/receiver unit, mainline valve
          assembly, and a tie-in from the proposed TL-669 pipeline to the existing LN-25, LN-35,
          and TL-400 pipelines. The proposed improvements will require an expansion of the
          existing gate site in Beaver County, PA.




                                                  -1-                                     Project Stratum
                                                                                          November 2026
 New Aboveground Facilities:
  • New Terrain M&R Facility and Pipeline Tap: install a new M&R facility in Lawrence County,
     PA, to include, but not be limited to, a dual-classified dekatherm building, meter building,
     regulation building, and associated gas quality and control equipment, such as ultrasonic
     metering, flow control, regulation equipment, underground headers, and various
     supporting facilities. Additionally, two new pipeline taps will be installed, one each on the
     existing LN-25 and LN-35 pipelines.
      •   Pine Mountain Gate Facility: install a new gate facility in Potter County, PA, to include a
          new tie-in from the proposed TL-668 pipeline to the existing LN-50 pipeline,
          launcher/receiver unit, mainline valve assembly, new permanent gravel pad and access
          road, various supporting equipment and facilities, and installation of perimeter fencing.
      •   Eaglerock Gate Facility: install a new gate facility in Beaver County, PA, to include a new
          tie-in from the proposed TL-669 pipeline to the existing LN-25 and LN-35 pipelines, a
          launcher/receiver unit, a new permanent gravel pad and access road, various supporting
          equipment and facilities, and installation of perimeter fencing.

EGTS will also consult with and obtain authorizations from relevant federal, state, and local
agencies. Construction of the Project is anticipated to begin in Quarter (Q)1 2028, pending receipt
of all necessary permits, authorizations, and approvals, and facilities will be placed into service
no later than Q4 2028.

In accordance with Title 18 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 380.12(d), Resource
Report 2 describes groundwater and surface waters in the Project area. The report provides
information used to evaluate potential impacts of the Project and identify measures to avoid,
minimize, and mitigate those impacts. EGTS identified the nature and location of surface waters,
wetlands, springs, wells, and point and non-point pollution sources using publicly available
information, consultation with appropriate agencies and landowners, and on-site field surveys
conducted from December 2025 through August 2026.

2.1       GROUNDWATER RESOURCES

2.1.1     Principal Aquifers

Groundwater occurs in saturated zones beneath the land surface, where it fills pores and fractures
in subsurface soil, sediment, and rock. An aquifer is a geologic formation, group of formations, or
part of a formation that contains sufficient saturated, permeable material to yield significant
quantities of water to wells and springs. Aquifers may be grouped into aquifer systems. A principal
aquifer is a regionally extensive aquifer or aquifer system that has the potential to be used as a
source of potable water (U.S. Geological Survey [USGS] 2003).

The proposed TL-669 pipeline, proposed Eaglerock Gate Facility, existing Koppel Junction, and
associated CYs are situated within the Pittsburgh Lower Plateau section of the Western Allegheny
Plateau Physiographic Province. Much of the Pittsburgh Lower Plateau section consists of shale,
siltstone, sandstone, limestone, and coal bedrock. Landforms consist of smooth to irregular,
undulating surfaces with narrow, relatively shallow valleys originating from fluvial erosion and
periglacial mass wasting.

The proposed TL-668 pipeline, existing Leidy Station, proposed Pine Mountain Gate facility, and
existing Greenlick Station are located within the Deep Valleys Section of the Appalachian Plateau


                                                -2-                                  Project Stratum
                                                                                     November 2026
 Physiographic Province. Landforms in this section consist of very deep, angular valleys and some
broad to narrow uplands which originate from fluvial erosion and periglacial mass wasting. The
existing Sabinsville Station is located within the Glaciated High Plateau Section of the
Appalachian Plateau Physiographic Province. The Glaciated High Plateau consists of broad to
narrow, rounded to flat, elongated uplands and shallow valleys originating from fluvial erosion,
glacial erosion, and glacial deposition (Sevon 2000).

Within the Appalachian Plateaus, groundwater occurs primarily in fractured bedrock aquifers
associated with sandstone, siltstone, shale, limestone, and coal of Permian-, Pennsylvanian-, and
Mississippian-age formations. Sandstone is generally the most productive water-bearing rock,
although coal beds and limestone locally yield groundwater. Groundwater in these bedrock
aquifers generally occurs within fractures, joints, and bedding-plane openings, and well yields
vary depending on the local geology and degree of fracturing (Trapp and Horn 1997). In PA,
reported typical yields of wells completed in the principal water-yielding geologic units range from
30 to 300 gallons per minute, with some wells yielding as much as 600 gallons per minute (Trapp
and Horn 1997). Aquifers within the Appalachian Plateaus are used for domestic, commercial,
industrial, mining, and thermoelectric power purposes.

2.1.2   Sole Source Aquifers

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) defines sole-source aquifers as aquifers
responsible for supplying 50 percent or more of the drinking water that is consumed in the area
overlying the aquifer. The designation requires that the USEPA review certain proposed projects
that are located within the sole-source aquifer’s designated area, thereby providing an additional
layer of protection to an area’s groundwater resources. Based on a review of the USEPA Region
3 list and mapping of designated sole source aquifers, no designated sole source aquifers occur
within the Project area (USEPA 2026a).

2.1.3   Well Head and Drinking Source Water Protection Areas

Amendments to the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) in 1986 established the Wellhead Protection
Program (WHPP), under which states develop programs to protect groundwater sources used by
public water systems. Section 1428(e) of the SDWA defines a Wellhead Protection Area (WHPA)
as “a surface and subsurface area surrounding a water well or wellfield, supplying a public water
system, through which contaminants are reasonably likely to move toward and reach such water
well or wellfield.” The size and delineation of a WHPA may be based on factors such as local
geology and groundwater flow characteristics or established according to state requirements for
the applicable public water system.

For the proposed Project, source water assessment information was reviewed for Beaver, Clinton,
Lawrence, Potter, and Tioga Counties. Public water systems within these counties obtain drinking
water from groundwater and surface-water sources, including wells, springs, streams, and rivers
(PADEP 2026). In Beaver County, the Beaver Falls Municipal Authority obtains its source water
from the Beaver River (Beaver Falls Municipal Authority 2026).

2.1.4   Public and Private Water Supply Wells and Springs

Based on information obtained from the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
(PADCNR) Bureau of Geological Survey’s PaGEODE – GEOlogic Data Exploration web-based



                                              -3-                                   Project Stratum
                                                                                    November 2026
 mapper, 34 water wells were identified within 150 feet of the proposed Project LODs (PADCNR
2026). The identified wells are summarized in Table 2.1.1-1. The PaGEODE database does not
include water wells used for public water supplies. No wells were identified within 150 feet of the
New Terrain M&R and Pipeline Tap Facility, Sabinsville Station, Pine Mountain Gate Facility, or
Eaglerock Gate Facility.

The potential for construction-related impacts on identified groundwater wells will depend on site-
specific conditions, including well location, well use, well construction, groundwater conditions,
and the nature and extent of proposed construction activities. Should follow-up testing identify a
potential reduction in groundwater quality or quantity that is attributable to Project construction,
EGTS will coordinate with the affected landowner to evaluate the concern and determine
appropriate next steps, which may include additional sampling or other corrective measures, as
warranted.

 2.1.6   Groundwater Construction and Operation Impacts and Mitigation

Construction activities, including clearing, grading, trench excavation, and localized dewatering,
could temporarily affect groundwater resources where construction activities encounter shallow
groundwater. Potential effects could include temporary changes in groundwater flow or localized
increases in turbidity. Accidental releases of fuels, lubricants, or other hazardous materials during
construction could also affect groundwater if a release reaches the subsurface. The potential for
these effects will depend on site-specific groundwater conditions and the depth and extent of
excavation.

The majority of pipeline construction will involve relatively shallow excavation. The maximum
anticipated trench excavation depth for the TL-668 and TL-669 pipeline segments is
approximately 20 feet. Based on available hydrogeologic information, groundwater is not
expected to be encountered during most pipeline construction activities. Where groundwater is
encountered, localized dewatering may be required and will be conducted in accordance with
applicable requirements. No blasting is anticipated as part of the Project.

EGTS will implement applicable spill prevention and response measures during construction in
accordance with a Preparedness, Prevention, and Contingency Plan (PPC Plan). The PPC Plan
will be maintained on site during construction. Measures will include appropriate equipment
inspections, spill prevention and containment procedures, and prompt containment and cleanup
of releases. Equipment and materials will be staged and refueling activities conducted in
accordance with applicable Project requirements and applicable federal and state regulations,
including maintaining appropriate setbacks from wetlands and waterbodies where practicable.

The Project has the potential to affect individual water supply wells if construction activities result
in a change in groundwater quality or quantity. If construction-related activities result in damage
to or loss of service from a potable water supply well, EGTS will provide an interim water supply,
as appropriate, and will repair or replace the affected well or otherwise compensate the affected
landowner, as appropriate. Appropriate corrective measures could include temporary filtration or
disinfection, well repair, or installation of a replacement well, depending on the nature and cause
of the impact.

Previously undocumented contaminated soil or groundwater could also be encountered during
construction. EGTS has prepared a Contaminated Media Plan, provided as Appendix 2-B of
Resource Report 2, to address the discovery and management of potentially contaminated media.
If potentially contaminated media are encountered, EGTS will manage the material in accordance
with the Contaminated Media Plan and applicable federal and state requirements, including
agency notification and appropriate handling, characterization, treatment, or disposal, as
applicable.

Operation and maintenance of the proposed Project facilities are not expected to result in
substantial impacts on groundwater resources. With implementation of the measures described
above and in the PPC Plan and Contaminated Media Plan, impacts on groundwater resources
are expected to be minor and localized.

2.2.5   Surface Water Construction and Operation Impacts and Mitigation

Approximately 8,870 linear feet of streams will be temporarily impacted during construction of the
proposed Project. Waterbody crossings may result in short-term, localized increases in turbidity
and sediment deposition associated with instream construction, trench dewatering, and erosion
from disturbed areas adjacent to stream channels. Potential impacts will be minimized through
implementation of the FERC Procedures, applicable federal and state waterbody crossing
permits, and Project-specific erosion and sediment (E&S) measures.

Prior to initiating each waterbody crossing, the adjacent construction ROW will be prepared to
minimize the duration of instream construction. To the extent practicable, stream crossings will
be constructed perpendicular to the direction of flow, and existing trees within riparian areas will
be retained where practicable. Construction activities will be conducted in a manner that maintains
stream flow and minimizes disturbance to the streambed and banks. Where necessary, pipe
installed beneath waterbodies and within floodplains will be weighted to prevent flotation.
Following installation, the trench will be backfilled with excavated material and the streambed and
banks will be restored to preconstruction contours and stable conditions.




                                              -12-                                  Project Stratum
                                                                                    November 2026
 ATWS may be required adjacent to waterbody crossings for construction staging, equipment, pipe
assembly, and material storage. In accordance with the FERC Procedures, ATWS will be located
at least 50 feet from the water's edge unless a site-specific modification is requested by EGTS
and approved by FERC. Locations where ATWS is proposed within 50 feet of a waterbody are
identified in Table 2.4.1-1 and will be subject to the applicable site-specific requirements.

EGTS will use flume or dam-and-pump dry-ditch crossing methods for the TL-668 and TL-669
pipeline waterbody crossings, as described below. Crossing methods will be implemented in
accordance with the FERC Procedures, any site-specific modifications approved by FERC, and
applicable requirements of federal and state waterbody crossing permits, including U.S. Army
Corps of Engineers (USACE) and PADEP authorizations (see Section 1.12 of Resource Report
1). These crossing methods will maintain water flow through the crossing area while the pipeline
trench is excavated and the pipeline is installed, thereby minimizing the duration and extent of
instream disturbance.

During clearing and grading, E&S measures, including silt fence, compost filter sock, or other
approved measures, will be installed and maintained along the construction ROW and ATWS
adjacent to waterbodies as required by the Project's applicable E&S requirements. E&S measures
will be maintained until disturbed areas are stabilized. Where necessary to accommodate
equipment access, linear sediment controls may be temporarily removed and replaced in
accordance with the Project's E&S requirements.

Mobile equipment refueling and lubrication will generally occur in upland areas at least 100 feet
from waterbodies and adjacent wetlands. Where site-specific construction requirements
necessitate refueling or operation of stationary equipment within 100 feet of a waterbody, EGTS
will implement the applicable measures in the PPC Plan. The PPC Plan will be maintained on
each construction spread during construction, as required by the FERC Procedures.

Following pipeline installation, waterbody crossings will be restored by backfilling the trench with
native excavated material and restoring the streambed profile and banks to preconstruction
contours and stable conditions. Larger rocks or boulders removed from the streambed will be
replaced, where practicable, following backfilling. Banks will be stabilized using appropriate
measures, which may include seeding, erosion control blankets, tree planting, or other approved
stabilization materials. Impervious trench breakers will be installed on each side of the waterbody
crossing. Slope breakers will be installed as needed based on slope, terrain, and PADEP
requirements. Temporary E&S measures will remain in place and will be inspected and
maintained until the disturbed areas are adequately stabilized and revegetated.

Operation of the Project is not expected to result in direct impacts to surface water resources.
Routine operation and maintenance activities will be conducted in accordance with applicable
federal and state requirements and will avoid or minimize disturbance to waterbodies.

Flume Method

The flume crossing method consists of isolating and temporarily diverting the flow of water across
the trenching area through one or more large-diameter, smooth flume pipes placed in the
waterbody. This method allows for trenching activities to occur beneath the flume pipes containing
the water flow thereby avoiding sedimentation and turbidity in the waterbody.




                                              -13-                                  Project Stratum
                                                                                    November 2026
 For each waterbody where the flume method is implemented, a sufficient number of adequately
sized flume pipes will be installed in the waterbody to accommodate the highest anticipated flows
during construction.

Prior to installation, EGTS will visually inspect the flume pipes to confirm that they are free of dirt,
grease, oil, or other pollutants. After placing the pipes in the waterbody, sand- or pea gravel-filled
bags, water bladders, or metal wing deflectors will be placed in the waterbody around the flume
pipes upstream and downstream of the proposed trench. These devices will serve to dam the
stream and divert the water flow through the flume pipes thereby isolating the water flow from the
construction work area between the dams.

After installation of the flume pipes, the remaining standing water between the dams will be
pumped out. Pump intakes will be appropriately screened to prevent entrainment of aquatic
species. Additionally, fish trapped in the dewatered area will be removed and returned to the
flowing waterbody. Leakage from the dams or subsurface flow from below the waterbody bed may
cause water to accumulate in the trench once trenching has begun. If water accumulates in this
area, it may be periodically pumped out and discharged into energy dissipation/sediment filtration
devices as required by the Procedures. Such devices include geotextile filter bags or straw bale
structures.

Equipment located on the banks of the waterbody will be used to excavate a trench under the
flume pipe across the dewatered streambed. Spoil excavated from the waterbody trench will be
placed and stored on the bank above the high-water mark and a minimum of 10 feet from the
edge of the waterbody. Once the trench is excavated, a prefabricated segment of pipe will be
installed beneath the flume pipes. The trench will then be backfilled with the native material
excavated from the trench across the waterbody bed. The banks will be stabilized before
removing the dams and flume pipes and returning flow to the waterbody channel.

The flume method has proven to be an effective technique for constructing pipelines across
sensitive waterbodies. The potential for the introduction of turbidity or suspended sediments is
limited because sediment generated during trench excavation and backfilling operations is
isolated to the dewatered area between dams. When flumes are installed properly, the operation
of the flume is generally stable and can be left in place for periods prior to and following the
installation of the waterbody pipeline crossing. The flume method also provides for continued fish
passage through the construction work area via the flume pipes during the crossing.

Dam-and-Pump Method

The dam-and-pump method may be used as an alternative to the flume method. The dam-and-
pump method is similar to the flume method except that pumps and hoses are used instead of
flume pipes to isolate and transport the stream flow around the construction work area. Similar to
the flume method, the objective of the dam-and-pump method is to create a relatively dry work
area to avoid or minimize the transportation of sediment and turbidity downstream of the crossing
during instream work.

As the first step in implementing the dam-and-pump method, one or more pumps and hoses of
sufficient size to transport anticipated flows around the construction work area will be installed in
the waterbody. Additional back-up pumps will be on site at all times in case of pump failure. Once
the pumps are operational, the waterbody upstream and downstream of the construction area will




                                                -14-                                    Project Stratum
                                                                                        November 2026
 be dammed. As the dams are installed, the pumps will be started to maintain continuous flow in
the waterbody.

Following the installation of the dams, the pumps will be run continuously until the pipeline is
installed across the waterbody and the streambed and banks are restored. Pump intakes above
the upstream dam will be appropriately screened to prevent entrainment of aquatic species.
Energy-dissipation devices will be used to prevent scouring of the streambed at the discharge
location.

Excavators located on the banks of the waterbody will be used to excavate a trench across the
waterbody. Spoil removed from the trench will be placed and stored on the bank above the high
water mark at a minimum of 10 feet from the edge of the waterbody. Trench plugs will be
maintained between the upland trench and the waterbody crossing. After backfilling, the dams
will be removed and the banks restored and stabilized as described above.

After the completion of construction, streambeds will be restored to their former elevations and
grades. Spoil, debris, pilings, cofferdams, construction materials, and any other obstructions
resulting from or used during the construction of the pipeline will be removed to prevent
interference with normal water flow and use. Any excavated material not used as backfill will be
disposed of in a manner and at locations satisfactory to the agencies having jurisdiction. Following
grading, all stream banks will be restored to prevent subsequent erosion, in accordance with
applicable permits and approvals.

2.3     WETLANDS

Wetlands, as defined by the USEPA and USACE, are “[t]hose areas that are inundated or
saturated by surface or ground water at a frequency and duration sufficient to support, and that
under normal circumstances do support, a prevalence of vegetation typically adapted for life in
saturated soil conditions” (USACE 1987). Field biologists conducted wetland delineations within
the Project survey area from December 2025 through August 2026 in accordance with the 1987
Corps of Engineers Wetlands Delineation Manual and the applicable Regional Supplements to
the Corps of Engineers Wetland Delineation Manual for the Eastern Mountains and Piedmont and
Northcentral and Northeast regions (USACE 2012). A detailed description of the wetland
delineation methodology and results is provided in the Waters Delineation Reports included in
Appendix 2-A. Wetlands were classified using the Cowardin Classification System (Cowardin et
al. 1979).

2.3.2    Wetland Construction and Operation Impacts

Approximately 0.803 acres of jurisdictional wetlands will be impacted by the proposed Project, of
which approximately 0.674 acres will be temporarily impacted. The remaining approximately
0.129 acres will be permanently impacted: approximately 0.023 acres of palustrine scrub-shrub
(PSS) wetlands associated with the TL-668 pipeline will be permanently converted to palustrine
emergent (PEM), and approximately 0.106 acres of PEM wetlands associated with the New
Terrain Facility and Pipeline Tap will be permanently filled and/or drained by construction of the
gravel pads for the new M&R facility and pipeline tap.

Construction within wetlands will be conducted in accordance with the FERC Procedures, site-
specific modifications to the FERC Procedures requested by EGTS and approved by FERC, and
applicable federal and state wetland crossing permit requirements. In accordance with the FERC
Procedures, the construction ROW through wetlands will be limited to 75 feet. ATWS may be
required on both sides of wetland crossings for construction staging, equipment and material
storage, pipe assembly, and storage of excavated spoil and will be located in upland areas at
least 50 feet from the wetland boundary, except where site-specific modifications are requested
by EGTS and approved by FERC. Locations where proposed ATWS does not meet the 50-foot
setback are identified in Table 2.4.1-1.




                                                    -17-                              Project Stratum

 Vegetation clearing within wetlands will be limited to the extent necessary for construction. Trees
and shrubs will be cut flush with the ground surface and removed from wetlands. Stump removal,
grading, topsoil segregation, and excavation will generally be limited to the trench area to
minimize disturbance to wetland soils and native seed and rootstock. Topsoil will be segregated
in wetlands where conditions are suitable for segregation and replacement.

E&S measures will be installed and maintained adjacent to wetlands and within ATWS, as
necessary, to minimize sediment transport from disturbed areas. Measures may include compost
filter sock, silt fence, or other approved controls. Sediment barriers will be installed at wetland
boundaries and along the base of slopes where necessary to prevent sediment from entering
wetlands. If trench dewatering is required, discharge will be conducted in accordance with
applicable permit requirements and using appropriate energy dissipation and sediment filtration
measures to minimize erosion and sedimentation.

Wetland contours and hydrology will be restored following pipeline installation. Where necessary
to maintain wetland hydrology, trench breakers will be installed at wetland boundaries and/or at
the base of slopes in accordance with the FERC Procedures. Where topsoil is segregated, subsoil
will be backfilled first, followed by replacement of the segregated topsoil. In wetlands underlain
by rocky soils, rock-free soil or sand will be used as padding around the pipeline, as necessary.
Equipment mats and geotextile materials used to facilitate construction access will be removed
following completion of construction activities.

Permanent slope breakers will be installed in upland areas adjacent to wetlands where necessary
to prevent sediment transport into wetlands. Temporary E&S measures will remain in place until
disturbed areas are adequately stabilized and revegetated, after which they will be removed and
properly disposed of.

Following construction, wetland areas will be restored and revegetated in accordance with the
FERC Procedures and applicable federal and state permit requirements. EGTS will comply with
the FERC Procedures for post-construction vegetation maintenance within and adjacent to
wetlands and waterbodies, including maintaining the required riparian and wetland vegetation
restrictions within the permanent ROW.

EGTS will implement the measures specified in the PPC Plan and applicable FERC Procedures
to minimize the potential for spills or releases to affect wetlands. If previously unidentified
contaminated media are encountered during Project activities, EGTS will implement the
procedures in the Unanticipated Contaminated Media Plan provided in Appendix 2-B.

Operation and routine maintenance of the Project are not expected to result in additional direct
impacts to wetlands beyond the permanent impacts identified above. Vegetation maintenance
within the permanent ROW will be conducted in accordance with the FERC Procedures and
applicable permit requirements.

                                     1.0 INTRODUCTION


Civil & Environmental Consultants, Inc. (CEC) conducted a waters delineation for the TL-669
Natural Gas Transmission Line (TL-669 pipeline) in Big Beaver Township, Beaver County,
Pennsylvania, which is associated with Eastern Gas Transmission and Storage, Inc.’s (EGTS)
Project Stratum (Figure 1).


Please refer to Figure 1 for the location of the TL-669 pipeline and an overview of Project Stratum.
The aboveground facilities and TL-668 Natural Gas Transmission Line, which are also part of
Project Stratum, are included in separate waters delineation reports: reports #1 and #2,
respectively.


This report includes the findings of a desktop data review and field delineation of the area of
interest (AOI) for the TL-669 pipeline portion of Project Stratum. The purpose was to identify,
characterize, and delineate wetlands, streams, and other waters located within the AOI. This report
presents the methodology and findings.




                                                 -1-                            CEC Project 356-834
                                                                                Revised October 2026
                                     2.0 METHODOLOGY


2.1       ENVIRONMENTAL DATA REVIEW


Prior to the field delineation, the following data sources were consulted to aid in the identification
of potential wetlands, streams, and other waters within the AOI:


      •   U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 7.5-minute topographic quadrangle maps;
      •   U.S. Department of Agriculture, Natural Resource Conservation Service (USDA-NRCS)
          Soil Survey Geographic (SSURGO) Database;
      •   Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) flood hazard data;
      •   U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) National Wetlands Inventory (NWI);
      •   USGS 3D Hydrography Program (3DHP);
      •   Publicly-available Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR)- derived topography; and
      •   Aerial imagery from various sources.


These publicly available data sources aided in overall habitat characterizations and facilitated
potential water resource identification within the AOI. Topographic depressions, mapped hydric
soils, mapped NWI resources, mapped 3DHP streams, and FEMA floodplains have higher
potential to contain wetlands, streams, and other surface water features.


2.2       FIELD METHODS


CEC performed a waters delineation to identify and delineate wetlands, streams, and other waters
within the AOI. The following sections outline the field methods used to delineate these waters.


2.2.1     Wetland Delineation


CEC ecologists identified, characterized, and delineated wetlands in accordance with the routine,
on-site determination methodology described in the Corps Manual, supplemented by the following
technical guidance documents:


                                                  -2-                             CEC Project 356-834
                                                                                  Revised October 2026
    •   Regional Supplement to the Corps of Engineers Wetland Delineation Manual:
       Northcentral and Northeast (Version 2.0) (USACE 2012); (referred to hereafter as
       Regional Supplement);
   •   National Wetland Plant List (USACE 2022); and
   •   Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the United States Version 9.0 (USDA-NRCS 2024).


CEC ecologists walked the AOI and collected data at representative locations within each plant
community cover type and areas with potential water features characteristics (e.g., localized
depressions, converging slopes, and evident hydrology). Data collected at each sampling point
were recorded on USACE Wetland Determination Data Sheets. The sampling plan was modified
as necessary if additional plant community cover types or potential water features characteristics
were encountered.


At each sampling point, the following parameters were assessed: vegetation, soils, and hydrology.
First, visual estimates of percent absolute cover of plant species were recorded for each of the
following strata, when present: tree, sapling/shrub, herb, and woody vine. A determination of
whether the plant community was dominated by hydrophytic (wetland) plants was then made using
the Rapid Test or Dominance Test indicators. Next, soils were sampled to determine if soils met
hydric soil indicators. Lastly, wetland hydrology indicators (e.g., surface water, high water table,
saturation, etc.) were recorded, if present.


The sampling point data was used to determine whether that point was located in a wetland or non-
wetland (i.e., upland). If a wetland was identified, further sampling was performed to delineate the
wetland/non-wetland boundary. Each wetland was also classified according to the NWI
classification system developed by the Federal Geographic Data Committee (2013) and Cowardin
et al. (1979). The primary wetland classifications included the following:


   •   Palustrine emergent wetland (PEM): rooted herbaceous and grass-like plants which
       stand erect above the water or ground surface characterize this wetland class (excluding
       mosses or lichens). Vegetation is present for most of the growing season in most years.
       Emergent wetlands include marshes, meadows, and fens.



                                                 -3-                            CEC Project 356-834
                                                                                Revised October 2026
    •   Palustrine scrub-shrub wetland (PSS): woody vegetation less than 20 feet tall dominate
       this wetland class. Plant species include true shrubs, young trees, and trees or shrubs that
       are small or stunted because of environmental conditions. Scrub-shrub wetlands include
       shrub swamps and bogs.
   •   Palustrine forested wetland (PFO): woody vegetation 20 feet or taller dominate this
       wetland class. Forested wetlands generally include an overstory of trees, an understory of
       young trees and shrubs, and an herbaceous layer.
   •   Palustrine unconsolidated bottom (PUB): nontidal wetland lacking vegetation but is less
       than 8 hectare (20 acres) in size with a water depth in the deepest part of basin less than
       2.5 meters (8.2 feet) at low water. Includes all wetlands and deepwater habitats with at least
       25 percent cover of particles smaller than stones (less than 6-7 centimeter), and a vegetative
       cover less than 30 percent.


If more than one Cowardin classification type was identified within a wetland, the boundary
between the types was delineated. Wetland boundaries were recorded using a mapping-grade
handheld Global Navigational Satellite System (GNSS) receiver capable of sub-meter accuracy.


Upland habitats were also recorded on USACE Wetland Determination Data Sheets. Upland
sampling points were documented adjacent to wetland delineation boundaries, as well as at
representative upland habitats throughout the AOI.

 2.2.2   Stream and Other Waters Delineation


Concurrent with the wetland delineation, CEC ecologists walked the AOI to identify streams and
other waters. These waters were evaluated for the presence of an OHWM in accordance with
USACE Regulatory Guidance Letter (RGL) No. 05-05: Ordinary High Water Mark Identification
(USACE 2005), USACE Interim National Ordinary High Water Mark Field Delineation Manual
for Rivers and Streams (USACE 2022), and definitions under 33 CFR 328. As described in these
OHWM guidance materials and 33 CFR 328.3(c)(4), an OHWM is established by a clear, natural
line impressed upon the bank, shelving, changes in the character of soil, destruction of terrestrial
vegetation, the presence of litter and debris, or other appropriate means that consider the
characteristics of the surrounding areas. Potential jurisdiction limits are delineated using OHWM
indicators as weight of evidence, including geomorphic (e.g. breaks in slope), transition of
vegetation types, changes in sediment type, and other indicators demarcating the regular high flow
surface water elevation (e.g. observed flow event, wrack of leaf litter disturbed or washed away).
The uppermost limit of an ephemeral stream was established where the stream loses its defined
bed and bank or OHWM.


In addition, all watercourses, which include streams, are defined in PA as “a channel or conveyance
of surface water having defined bed and banks” (PA Code 2022). The federal and state guidance
were applied to determine the extents of streams.


For streams, physical and biological data were used to infer the stream’s hydrologic flow regime,
using a weight-of-evidence approach. CEC used field indicators such as flow, substrate
composition, presence of defined bed and bank, origin of hydrologic sources, presence/absence of
vegetation within the stream channel, and presence/absence of benthic macroinvertebrates, fish,
and other aquatic biota to classify onsite stream segments into one of three stream types:


   •    Ephemeral: surface water flows or pools only in direct response to precipitation (e.g., rain
        or snow fall);




                                                  -5-                           CEC Project 356-834
                                                                                Revised October 2026
    •   Intermittent: surface water flows continuously during certain times of the year and more
       than in direct response to precipitation (e.g., seasonally when the groundwater table is
       elevated or when snowpack melts); and
   •   Perennial: surface water flows continuously year-round during normal rainfall. Ground
       water provides the primary hydrology.


Stream boundaries were located using a mapping-grade GNSS receiver capable of sub-meter
accuracy. The physical characteristics of the streams and field observations were summarized on
field data forms.

                                         3.0 RESULTS


3.1     ENVIRONMENTAL DATA REVIEW


The USGS 7.5-minute topographic quadrangle, NWI data, and USGS 3D Hydrography Program
(3DHP) data did not identify mapped streams within the AOI (Figure 2). No FEMA-mapped 100-
year floodplains or floodways occur within the AOI. A review of aerial imagery likewise did not
indicate defined channel features within the AOI. Publicly available LiDAR data, however,
indicated the presence of up to four streams within the northwest portion of the AOI (Figure 3).


The NWI data did not identify wetlands within the AOI (Figure 2), but a review of aerial imagery
indicated the presence of a ponded area in the northwest portion of the AOI. The SSURGO data
identified eight soil mapping units within the AOI. None of the soils were rated as hydric, but one
soil layer was somewhat poorly drained (Table 1 and Figure 2).


3.2     FIELD RESULTS


CEC staff conducted a field delineation on November 26, November 28, 2025, and February 19,
2026, to identify, delineate, and classify wetlands, streams, and other waters within the AOI. The
AOI consisted of existing natural gas pipeline right-of-way, hayfields, and forested areas.


3.2.1   Wetland Delineation


Eleven wetlands were delineated within the AOI. Wetlands were classified as palustrine emergent
(PEM) or palustrine unconsolidated bottom (PUB). Refer to Table 2 for a summary of the wetlands
delineated in the AOI and Figure 3 for the location of the wetlands and sampling points.
Photographs and Wetland Determination Data Forms are found in Appendix A and B, respectively.

 3.2.2   Stream and Other Waters Delineation


Four streams were delineated within the AOI. Each one corresponded with the areas indicative of
streams on LiDAR topography. Three were classified as intermittent, and one was classified as
having both intermittent and ephemeral reaches. All streams were unnamed tributaries (UNTs) to
Stockman Run. Refer to Table 3 for a summary of the streams delineated in the AOI and Figure 3
for the location of the streams.


Additionally, three erosional features were identified within the AOI. These features convey runoff
during storm events but lack sufficient hydrology and characteristics such as defined bed and bank
and OHWM to be classified as streams. Refer to Table 4 for a summary of the erosional features
found in the AOI and Figure 3 for the location of these features.


Photographs of the streams and erosional features are included in Appendix A. Stream data forms
are found in Appendix C.

                           5.0 REGULATORY CONSIDERATIONS


The USACE has authority to permit the discharge of dredged or fill material into Waters of the
U.S. (WOTUS) under Section 404 of the federal Clean Water Act, and to permit work and the
placement of structures in navigable waters under Sections 9 and 10 of the Rivers and Harbors Act
of 1899. Wetlands, streams, and other waters that meet the guidelines contained in the Corps
Manual, Regional Supplement, and Regulatory Guidance Letter No. 05-05 are subject to regulation
by USACE as WOTUS as defined by 33 CFR 328.3(a), and the currently in effect regulatory
definition (SCOTUS 2023).


As a result of ongoing litigation with the January 2023 Revised Definition of ‘Waters of the United
States’ Rule (2023 WOTUS Rule), federal agencies will implement the 2023 WOTUS Rule, as
amended by the conforming rule, in 23 states including PA, the District of Columbia, and the U.S.
Territories. In the other 27 states and for certain parties, the agencies are interpreting "WOTUS"
consistent with the pre-2015 regulatory regime and the Supreme Court's decision in Sackett v.
Environmental Protection Agency (May 24, 2023) until further notice.


If CWA Section 404 authorization and/or other federal permits are required for the proposed
project, consultation with the USFWS will likely be required pursuant to Section 7 of the
Endangered Species Act. Furthermore, consultation with the State Historic Preservation Office
may also be required relative to potential effects to resources listed on or eligible for listing on the
National Register of Historic Places.


The PA Department of Environmental Protection (PADEP) has coinciding jurisdiction over
“waters of the Commonwealth” as established by the Dam Safety and Encroachments Act (P.L.
1375, No. 325) and the Clean Streams Law (P.L. 1987, No. 3941). The PA Code of State
Regulations, in Title 25, Chapter 105 Dam Safety and Waterway Management, defines “waters of
the Commonwealth” as any watercourse, stream, waterbody, or wetland, including their
floodways. Like the USACE, the PADEP generally considers channels to be potentially
jurisdictional if they exhibit defined bed and banks, whether natural or artificial, with perennial or
intermittent flow. The PADEP regulates encroachments, defined as “any structure or activity

 which changes, expands or diminishes the course, current or cross section of a watercourse,
floodway, or body of water” through the Chapter 105 permit process. The floodway is defined as
extending 50 feet from the top of bank of watercourses if not delineated by a Federal
Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) study.


In PA, the USACE has delegated authority to the PADEP to authorize minor qualifying activities
through the state-wide Section 404 permit titled PA State Programmatic General Permit 7
(PASPGP-7), with concurrent review by USACE for certain categories of impacts. A Joint Permit
Application to PADEP and USACE is typically required for activities with more significant
impacts that exceed the thresholds of PA Chapter 105 General Permits and PASPGP-7. In addition
to encroachments, permits for discharges to waters, including from construction stormwater runoff
or erosion, may be required by National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) and
PA Chapter 102 regulations.


Waters within the AOI were delineated using guidelines set forth by the PADEP and USACE,
which have final regulatory authority on the jurisdiction and extents of wetlands, streams, and
other waters.


It is the responsibility of any party that intends to discharge dredge or fill material into
WOTUS and/or isolated waters to comply with all applicable regulations.
